Here's how the recommended scenario level is calculated in Frosthaven:

> At recommended difficulty, the scenario level is equal to the average level of the characters divided by 2 (rounded up).

**Example from the rulebook:** If all characters are level 2, the average level (2) ÷ 2 = 1, so the scenario is still level 1. Only once a character reaches level 3 would the scenario level potentially increase.

---

**A few important notes:**

- The scenario level can always be set to any number from **0–7** at the start of a scenario, regardless of the recommendation. Lower if your party is struggling; higher if you want more challenge.
- **Solo mode** (or the **Open Information** variant): Add 1 to the average character level *before* dividing by 2 and rounding up. For example, three level 4 characters normally gives scenario level 2, but in solo mode it becomes ((4+1)÷2, rounded up) = 3.

**What the scenario level affects:**

| Scenario Level | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Monster Level | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
| Gold Conversion | 2 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
| Trap Damage | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9 |
| Hazardous Terrain | 1 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 3 | 4 |
| Bonus Experience | 4 | 6 | 8 | 10 | 12 | 14 | 16 | 18 |

*(Rulebook, p. 16)*

Here's how *advantage* works with attack modifier cards in Frosthaven:

## Advantage — Core Rule

> With advantage, the attacker draws two modifiers and uses one of them. A monster always uses the better one, but a character may use either one.

## Rolling Modifiers with Advantage

If the **first** card drawn is a *rolling modifier*, the process extends:

1. Keep drawing cards one at a time until you draw a non-rolling modifier.
2. Then draw **one more** card (ignore any rolling icon on this final card).
3. You now compare the first non-rolling modifier and the final card — use all the initial rolling modifiers **plus** whichever of those last two you choose.

If the **second** card drawn is a rolling modifier (but the first wasn't), the rolling icon on that second card is still ignored.

## Ambiguity

When it's unclear which modifier is "better" (e.g., one has an elemental infusion or a condition with no numeric value), any non-numeric effect is considered to have a **positive but undefined value**. If ambiguity remains, the attacker must use the card drawn **first**.

## Advantage + Disadvantage Cancel Out

> An attack cannot gain multiple instances of advantage or disadvantage. If an attack has both advantage and disadvantage, it is considered to have neither.

## Ranged Attacks on Adjacent Enemies

Any ranged attack targeting an adjacent enemy **automatically gains** *disadvantage* — so if you also have a source of *advantage*, the two cancel out and you draw normally.

---

*Source: Frosthaven Rulebook, passages 96–97*

Here is what *Poison* does in Frosthaven:

> **Poison:** All attacks targeting the figure gain "+1 Attack." Poison is removed when the figure is healed but, unlike *Wound*/*Brittle*/*Bane*, poison prevents the heal from increasing the figure's current hit point value.

**Key points to remember:**

- **Offensive debuff:** Every attack made against a *Poisoned* figure gets +1 to its attack value — this applies to all attackers, including other monsters.
- **Removed by healing:** A *Heal* ability will remove *Poison*, but the hit point restoration is **blocked** if *Poison* is present. The heal clears the condition without actually restoring any HP.
- **No duration:** Unlike conditions such as *Muddle* or *Stun*, *Poison* does **not** expire at the end of a turn — it persists until the figure is healed.

*Source: Frosthaven Rulebook, passage 101 (Negative Conditions)*

Here are the steps for a **long rest** in Frosthaven, as stated in the rulebook (passage 125):

**When to declare it:** During the **Card Selection** step, instead of playing two cards. The long rest counts as the character's entire turn for the round and is performed on **initiative 99**.

**Requirement:** The character must have **at least two cards** in their discard pile.

---

**Steps performed (in order):**

1. **Lose one card of their choice** from their discard pile, then return all remaining discarded cards to their hand. *(mandatory)*
2. **Perform "*Heal* 2, self."** *(optional)*
3. **Recover all spent items.** Items can even be used during the same turn they are recovered. *(optional)*

---

A few key points to keep in mind:
- Unlike a *short rest*, you **choose** which card you lose (rather than losing one at random).
- The long rest replaces your normal turn entirely — you do not play any ability cards that round.

Here's a full breakdown of **looting** in Frosthaven:

---

## The *Loot* Ability

> "*Loot X* is an ability that allows a figure to loot all loot tokens and treasure tiles within range X, including any in their current hex. This ability is unaffected by the presence of figures or overlay tiles. If there are no loot tokens or treasure tiles within the specified range, the ability cannot be performed."

*(Rulebook, passage 111)*

---

## Looting Loot Tokens

When a loot token is looted, it is removed from the map. What happens next depends on who looted it:

- **Monsters:** Nothing else happens.
- **Characters:** Draw one card from the **loot deck** (unless the deck is empty).

### Loot Card Types
Each scenario has a custom loot deck built from four types of cards:

| Type | Details |
|---|---|
| **Money** | 20 cards showing 1–3 coins; converted to gold based on scenario level |
| **Material Resources** | 8 cards per material type (lumber, metal, hide); amount varies by number of characters |
| **Herb Resources** | 2 cards per herb type (arrowvine, axenut, corpsecap, flamefruit, rockroot, snowthistle); provides 1 herb each |
| **Random Item** | 1 card; provides a random item drawn from the random item deck (can only be gained once per scenario) |

- **Money and resources** are **not gained until the end of the scenario**.
- **Random items** are gained **immediately** when looted and can be used for the rest of the scenario, even if it puts the character over the item limit.
- If the random item deck is empty, the card counts as a money card worth **three coins**.

---

## Looting Treasure Tiles

When a treasure tile is looted, it is removed from the map. **Monsters cannot loot treasure tiles.** If the tile is a **numbered treasure**, reference the Treasure Index and apply the effect — only the looting character gains the reward (unless it is a random item blueprint or random scenario).

---

## Key Notes

- *Loot* range is unaffected by figures or overlay tiles.
- Certain events can add a **+** sticker to a loot card, providing one additional resource of that type.
- If a character gains an item they cannot keep for any reason, they must give it to another character or sell it immediately.

*(Rulebook, passages 111–112 and passage 67)*

---

**Declaring a Long Rest**

During the **Card Selection** step, instead of selecting two ability cards, a character may declare a long rest — but only if they have **at least two cards in their discard pile**. A long rest constitutes their **entire turn for the round** and is performed on **initiative 99**.

---

**Long Rest Steps (in order):**

1. **Lose one card of their choice** from their discard pile and return the remaining cards to their hand. *(mandatory)*
2. **Perform "*Heal* 2, self"** *(optional)*
3. **Recover all spent items** *(optional)* — items can even be used during the same turn they are recovered.

---

**Key Points:**
- A long rest replaces playing cards entirely — no ability cards are played that round.
- You choose **which card to lose**, unlike a short rest where the lost card is random.
- The character acts on initiative **99**, meaning almost everything else goes before them.

*(Rulebook, passage 125)*

Here's how *Advantage* works with attack modifier cards in Gloomhaven (2nd Edition):

## Advantage — Basic Rule

> With **advantage**, the attacker draws two modifiers and uses one of them. A monster always uses the better one, but a character may use either one.

*(Rulebook, passage 103)*

---

## When Rolling Modifiers Are Involved

The process gets a bit more involved if rolling modifiers appear:

> If the first draw with advantage or disadvantage is a rolling modifier, the attacker draws additional modifiers, one at a time, until a non-rolling modifier is drawn. **They then draw one more modifier and ignore any rolling icon on it.**

So you keep drawing until you hit a non-rolling card, then draw **one final card** (ignoring any rolling icon on that last one). You now have two "final" cards to compare.

> If the attack has advantage, the attacker uses all initial rolling modifiers and whichever of the last two modifiers they choose.

---

## Summary of the Full Process

1. Draw cards one at a time until you get your **first non-rolling modifier**.
2. Draw **one more card** (its rolling icon is ignored).
3. All the rolling modifiers from step 1 **are applied** to the attack.
4. From the two non-rolling results, **a character may pick either one**; a monster must use the better one.

---

## Key Contrast with *Disadvantage*

With *disadvantage*, the process is the same draw sequence, but the initial rolling modifiers are **discarded** (not applied), and the attacker must use whichever of the last two cards is **worse**.

*(Rulebook, passage 103)*

Here's how the recommended scenario level is calculated in Gloomhaven (2nd Edition):

> **Recommended Scenario Level = Average Character Level ÷ 2 (rounded up)**

> **(Average Character Level + 1) ÷ 2 (rounded up)**

For example, three level 4 characters in standard play would give scenario level **2** ((4+4+4)÷3÷2), but in solo mode it would be **3** (((4+4+4)÷3+1)÷2).

Here's a full breakdown of **looting** in Gloomhaven (2nd Edition):

---

## The *Loot* Ability

> **"Loot X"** is an ability that allows a figure to loot all money tokens and treasure tiles within range X, including any in their current hex. This ability is unaffected by the presence of figures or overlay tiles. If there are no money tokens or treasure tiles within the specified range, the ability cannot be performed.

*(Rulebook, passage 132)*

---

## End-of-Turn Looting

> Characters must loot any money tokens or treasure tiles present in their hex **at the end of their turn**. No figures besides characters perform end-of-turn looting.

*(Rulebook, passage 156)*

Note: end-of-turn looting applies at the **end of the full turn**, not at the end of each movement.

---

## What Happens When You Loot

**Money tokens:**
- The token is removed from the map.
- If looted by a **monster**, nothing further happens.
- If looted by a **character**, they place the token on their character mat.

**Treasure tiles:**
- The tile is removed from the map.
- **Monsters cannot loot treasure tiles.**
- If it is a **numbered treasure**, reference its number in the Treasure Index and apply the effect.
- Only the looting character gains the reward (unless it is a random item design or random scenario).
- If the looting character gains a duplicate item they already own, they must **give it to another character or sell it immediately**.

*(Rulebook, passage 133)*

---

## Monster Loot Abilities

Monsters do not perform end-of-turn looting, but some monsters have explicit loot abilities on their ability cards. In those cases:
- The monster loots all **money tokens** within the specified range, removing them from the map.
- Those money tokens are **not** dropped by the monster when it dies.
- Monsters are **unable** to loot treasure tiles even with a loot ability.

*(Rulebook, passage 182)*

Great question — this scenario is directly addressed by both the rulebook and the FAQ. Here's how it resolves:

## The Monster Stays Put and Attacks at Disadvantage

### Why it won't walk through the traps

The rulebook is clear:

> "Monsters always prioritize a path that triggers the fewest negative hexes, even when that means not maximizing targets… Monsters only trigger negative hexes when there is no other viable path to attack an enemy."

The FAQ reinforces this with an important clarification:

> "A monster's first focus priority is to choose a hex from which they can attack an enemy, using the least possible movement, preferring 'safe' paths of any length over any paths with negative hexes. They will choose a safer path even if it's much longer, and even if it means they can't attack their focus this turn. They will only choose a path with one or more negative hexes if it's the only way to attack any enemy, **ever**, looking at the current state of the board, pretending the monster has infinite movement."

In your scenario, the monster **already has a valid attack path** (attack from its current hex at disadvantage). Because a safe path exists that lets it attack *at some point*, it will **never** move through traps.

### Why it won't move away to lose disadvantage

The rulebook states that a ranged monster will try to move away from an adjacent target to avoid disadvantage — **but** the FAQ clarifies:

> "If the monster would lose disadvantage by moving away from its focus, **if it can do so with its current movement, and if it can do so without entering a negative hex**, it will."

Since the only way to create distance requires moving through traps (negative hexes), the monster **won't move to shed the disadvantage** either.

### Result

The monster stays where it is and performs its ranged attack against your adjacent character **at** *disadvantage*. It will not enter the traps under any circumstances as long as a trap-free attack path exists.

*(Rulebook passage 175; FAQ passages 39–40)*

Section books are entirely game-specific. The number "67.1" is just a label used to index a physical card or page within one game's sticker/section book. > **Poison:** All attacks targeting the figure gain "+1 [Attack Modifier draw]." Poison is removed when the figure is healed but, unlike *Wound*, poison prevents the heal from increasing the figure's current hit point value.
